Title: A hybrid TOPSIS-agent-based framework for reducing the water demand requested by stakeholders with considering the agents’ characteristics and optimization of cropping pattern
Authors: Mahboubeh Ghazali; Tooraj Honar; Mohammad Reza Nikoo
Geographical_Context: Doroudzan irrigation and drainage network, Fars Province, Iran; six management regions downstream of Doroudzan Dam
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Crop planning; Deficit irrigation; Agricultural policy and farm economics
Study_Objective: Reduce agricultural water demand requested by heterogeneous stakeholders by combining agent-specific TOPSIS-informed behavioural modelling with management tools, then optimise cropping patterns under deficit irrigation to sustain farmer income across wet, normal and drought conditions.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Coordinate farmer water-demand reduction under limited government allocations while preserving economic viability through crop-pattern optimisation.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Decision-support/optimisation framework; Coordination/policy mechanism
Agent_Types: Agricultural/farmer agents aggregated by village; government/state agent
Agent_Roles: Agricultural agents request irrigation water and are classified as cooperative or non-cooperative according to demand versus allocation; government defines optimal/allocatable water and applies training, incentives, penalties and enforcement; the optimisation layer redesigns crop areas.
Decision_Mechanism: TOPSIS-derived agent-specific behavioural coefficients; cooperative/non-cooperative utility rules; government management interventions; genetic-algorithm crop-pattern optimisation under deficit irrigation
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each agricultural agent has locally determined water demand and behavioural response based on demographic, social, cultural and economic characteristics and neighbour influence, but decisions are constrained by government allocation and enforcement.
Input_Information: Existing cropping patterns; allocatable water by region; demographic, social, cultural and economic characteristics; expert judgements; neighbour composition; training/incentive/penalty parameters; crop prices/costs; crop-water production functions; rainfall, evapotranspiration, soil-water and irrigation-efficiency parameters
MAS_Platform_Technology: Hybrid TOPSIS–agent-based model; genetic-algorithm optimisation implemented in MATLAB
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Abstract; Sec. 2 Methodology; Sec. 2.1 Agent-based model; Sec. 2.2 TOPSIS; Sec. 2.3 Optimisation of cropping pattern; Fig. 1–2
Coordination_Mechanism: Hierarchical government allocation and management tools; neighbour/social-norm influence on cooperation; TOPSIS-personalised behavioural response; GA-based coordinated crop-pattern optimisation
Communication_Mechanism: Neighbour/social-norm influence plus government policy/management signals; no formal agent message protocol is reported.
Information_Shared: Neighbour cooperation/non-cooperation status; government water-allocation targets; management interventions; agent demographic/social/economic characteristics used to parameterise behavioural response
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water allocation and demand; cultivated crop area/cropping pattern
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Reduce requested irrigation water to near the government-defined allocatable amount while maximising/maintaining farmer net income and feasible crop production.
Conflict_Resolution: Training and incentives reinforce cooperative behaviour; penalties and executive/judicial enforcement constrain non-cooperative agents; crop-pattern optimisation reconciles water limits with farm-income objectives.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Water demands from 67 village-level agricultural agents across six management regions compete with limited reservoir allocation.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Existing crop areas and crop choices; government allocatable water; crop evapotranspiration and rainfall; soil-water balance; irrigation efficiencies; crop-water production functions; climatic condition (wet/normal/drought); economic costs/prices
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 2 Methodology; Sec. 2.1 ABM; Sec. 2.3 crop-pattern optimisation; Sec. 2.4 case study; Fig. 2
Agricultural_Outcomes: Optimised crop patterns increase cultivated area in most regions and are reported to increase net farm income and employment while maintaining strategic/regionally permitted crops.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Large reduction in the gap between farmer-requested water and allocatable water; deficit-irrigation crop optimisation further maintains the demand reduction while improving land use and income.
Environmental_Outcomes: Reduced agricultural pressure on scarce irrigation water under wet, normal and drought conditions.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Agent-specific demand management through social/policy tools combined with deficit irrigation and crop-pattern optimisation.
Quantitative_Results: Before ABM, requested water exceeded allocatable water by 7.6%, 18.2% and 45% in wet, normal and drought conditions; after ABM the excess fell to 1.37%, 3.5% and 1.09%. After ABM, total requested water remained 4.98, 10.21 and 2.55 MCM above allocation in wet/normal/drought conditions. Optimised cultivated area increased by about 15,419 ha in wet conditions, 25,168 ha in normal conditions (except region 2), and 4,169 ha in drought conditions (except region 3).
Tradeoffs_Reported: Water-demand reduction is balanced against farmer income, employment, food-security crop constraints and locally preferred high-water crops such as rice.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3 Results; Sec. 4 Discussion; Sec. 5 Conclusions; Tables 5–7; Figs. 6–8
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Comparative scenario evaluation; Optimisation
Evaluation_Environment: Hybrid ABM/TOPSIS/GA model applied to six management regions of the Doroudzan irrigation and drainage network.
Data_Source: Fars Regional Water Organization reports; existing cropping patterns and water requirements; demographic/social/economic/cultural village data; expert viewpoints; agronomic and irrigation parameters from regional records and literature
Experimental_Scenarios: Wet, normal and drought climatic conditions; before-versus-after ABM demand; existing versus optimised cropping patterns.
Baselines_Comparators: Farmer-requested water before ABM and existing cropping patterns; government-defined allocatable water serves as the allocation target.
Evaluation_Metrics: Requested-water excess above allocation (% and MCM); cultivated area; crop mix; net income; employment; optimisation feasibility
Evaluation_Results: The hybrid behavioural model sharply reduced requested-water excess under all three climate conditions; GA crop-pattern optimisation increased cultivated area in most regions and was reported to increase income/employment while sustaining water-demand reduction.
Evaluation_Scale: 67 agricultural/village agents plus government across six management regions; Doroudzan network includes 56,000 ha irrigated area and 30,356 ha net irrigated area in surveyed villages.
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Other — static behavioural model; Other — behavioural/mental-map specification
Reported_Limitations: Accurate prediction requires better empirical behavioural functions and mental maps for farmers; the implemented ABM is static and does not model multi-time-step behavioural dynamics.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Develop empirically grounded behavioural functions/mental maps and dynamic multi-period agent models, then validate management responses under real operational conditions.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 2.4 Case study; Sec. 3 Results; Sec. 4 Discussion; Sec. 5 Conclusions
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B07). Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: Fine spatio-temporal simulation of cropping and farming systems effects on irrigation withdrawal dynamics within a river basin
Authors: Clément Murgue; Romain Lardy; Maroussia Vavasseur; Delphine Leenhardt; Olivier Therond
Venue: 7th International Congress on Environmental Modelling and Software (iEMSs 2014)
Geographical_Context: Downstream Aveyron River watershed, southwest France; irrigated basin of more than 800 km² with about 40,000 ha usable agricultural area
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Cropping-system planning; River-basin water management; Agricultural decision modelling
Study_Objective: Develop and assess a fine spatio-temporal agricultural model within MAELIA that reproduces farmer crop/irrigation decisions and withdrawal dynamics so alternative cropping-system distributions and water-management strategies can be designed and assessed under water scarcity.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate farm-level irrigation decisions and their basin-scale hydrological consequences to support participatory design and assessment of cropping-system and water-management alternatives.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; MAS platform component; Decision-support/participatory assessment framework
Agent_Types: Farmer agents; agricultural fields/cropping blocks; irrigation blocks; hydrological resource entities; normative/regulatory components
Agent_Roles: Farmer agents apply crop-management and irrigation decision rules at field/farm level; field/block entities represent crop and irrigation organisation; hydrological components update rivers/aquifers/dams; normative components impose water-use restrictions.
Decision_Mechanism: Daily crop-management and irrigation decision rules triggered by crop/soil state, climate/forecast, water-resource levels and regulatory restrictions; farm-level irrigation-block/turn organisation
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each virtual farmer autonomously manages its fields using crop- and irrigation-specific decision rules, while decisions are constrained by shared hydrological conditions and normative withdrawal restrictions.
Input_Information: LPIS field/farm geography; crop rotations and management strategies; soils/topography; daily temperature, precipitation and evapotranspiration; water-resource topology/levels; hydraulic infrastructure; crop state; rainfall/forecast indicators; water-use restrictions
MAS_Platform_Technology: MAELIA multi-agent platform; GIS/LPIS spatial data; SWAT-based surface- and groundwater hydrology
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Introduction; Sec. 2.1 Overall description and concepts; Sec. 2.3 system structure; Sec. 2.4–2.6 decision/irrigation components
Coordination_Mechanism: Farm-level irrigation-block scheduling plus environment-mediated coordination through shared hydrological resources and normative water-use restrictions.
Communication_Mechanism: Shared-state/environment-mediated interaction via MAELIA hydrological and normative models; no direct farmer-to-farmer message protocol is reported.
Information_Shared: Water-resource availability; regulatory withdrawal restrictions; crop/soil state; weather/forecast information; farm/field irrigation status
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation withdrawals from rivers, aquifers and dams; irrigation timing and farm-level crop-management tasks
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Represent and manage agricultural withdrawals so alternative farming organisations can be assessed against river-basin water-scarcity/low-flow constraints.
Conflict_Resolution: Normative water-use restrictions and shared hydrological feedback constrain farmer withdrawals; alternative management designs are intended to be co-designed and assessed with stakeholders.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Withdrawals by many irrigated farms/fields compete for limited river, aquifer and dam water, particularly during low-flow periods.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Crop phenology and management rule; soil/pedoclimatic conditions; recent precipitation; weather forecast; water-resource levels; regulatory restrictions; irrigation-block structure and turn duration
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Introduction; Sec. 2.1; Sec. 2.5 irrigation organisation; Sec. 3.2–3.4 withdrawal/irrigation results
Agricultural_Outcomes: The model reproduces interannual and daily irrigation-practice patterns, including first/last irrigation dates, number of irrigation turns and seasonal dose for major irrigated crops.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: No direct efficiency improvement is claimed; the model provides a validated basis for designing cropping/water-management alternatives and reproduces withdrawal volumes and source shares sufficiently closely for assessment.
Environmental_Outcomes: Supports analysis of agricultural pressure on river-basin low flows and withdrawals from rivers, aquifers and dams.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Participatory redesign of cropping-system spatial distributions and water-management strategies, evaluated through coupled agricultural–hydrological simulation.
Quantitative_Results: For 2003–2010, simulated annual withdrawals differed from agency-reported volumes by an average of about -10%, with a maximum -23% difference in the extreme 2003 drought. Average simulated versus observed source shares were aquifers 17% vs 10%, dams 23% vs 30%, rivers 60% vs 60%. Experts estimated omitted pipe/field losses could require a 15–20% upward adjustment to withdrawals.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Core management trade-off is agricultural irrigation demand versus maintenance of scarce river-basin water/low-flow conditions; no formal multi-objective trade-off optimisation is reported.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3.2 Annual balance; Sec. 3.3 withdrawal dynamics; Sec. 3.4 field-level irrigation practices; Conclusions
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Model validation; Comparative empirical validation
Evaluation_Environment: Eight-year MAELIA simulation of the downstream Aveyron socio-agro-hydrological system using observed climatic forcing.
Data_Source: French LPIS 2006–2009; regional water-basin agency mandatory withdrawal reports; observed climate 2003–2010; soil/topographic/hydraulic data; local expert knowledge; irrigation-practice survey of 27 farms; SWAT hydrology inputs
Experimental_Scenarios: Observed climatic sequence 2003–2010, including the extreme 2003 drought; evaluation at basin, hydrological-unit and field/practice scales.
Baselines_Comparators: Regional water-basin agency reported annual withdrawals and source shares; farm-survey irrigation practices.
Evaluation_Metrics: Annual withdrawal volume error; interannual dynamics; source-share distribution; first/last irrigation dates; number of irrigation turns; irrigation dose; qualitative fit to observed practices
Evaluation_Results: Annual withdrawal dynamics are reproduced with about 10% average error, but 2003 extreme-drought withdrawals are underestimated by 23%; rivers are reproduced accurately while aquifer/dam shares differ by about 7 percentage points; maize/fruit irrigation practices are reproduced most accurately.
Evaluation_Scale: More than 800 km² watershed; ~1,150 farms (43% irrigated); ~15,000 geolocated fields; ~40,000 ha usable agricultural area; eight simulated years.
Limitation_Categories: Environmental modelling; Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Adoption/usability
Reported_Limitations: Decision rules are not robust enough for extreme climatic events; pipe leaks and on-field evaporation losses are omitted; withdrawals for some crops are underestimated; integrating locally validated subcomponents into one model may still trigger stakeholder distrust.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Use longer climate time series; add adaptive decision rules for extreme drought; represent conveyance/field losses; improve underrepresented crop practices; develop stakeholder-interaction strategies that stress transparency and model weaknesses.
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B09). Part of the MAELIA research line already represented in the corpus; exact Study_Family_ID deferred to Step 5.

Title: Agent-based spatial models applied to agriculture: a simulation tool for technology diffusion, resource use changes and policy analysis
Geographical_Context: Empirical agricultural region in Chile; Mercosur policy context; approximately 667 km²
Agricultural_Domain: Crop and farm management; Agricultural technology adoption; Land and water markets; Irrigation; Agricultural policy
Study_Objective: Develop and test a spatial multi-agent/cellular-automata model that represents heterogeneous farm-household decisions, innovation diffusion, inter-household land/water exchanges and hydrological feedback for agricultural policy analysis.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Explore how decentralised farm decisions, social diffusion, imperfect land/water markets and irrigation feedback generate regional technology adoption, structural change and policy outcomes.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Methodological framework; Policy-evaluation framework
Agent_Types: Farm-household agents; spatial farm-parcel/cellular entities; hydrological sections/resource entities
Agent_Roles: Farm households make investment, production, consumption, tenure and technology-adoption decisions; exchange information and land/water rights; spatial/hydrological entities represent parcels, freshwater allocation and irrigation return flows.
Decision_Mechanism: Recursive/mixed-integer farm programming; sequential sub-optimisation with feedback; technology-adoption thresholds and frequency-dependent diffusion; endogenous land/water market auctions; irrigation return-flow rules
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each of 5,400 farm households solves its own decision problems autonomously and adapts from prior experience, while interacting with neighbours through innovation diffusion, resource markets and spatial/hydrological feedback.
Input_Information: Farm resources and household constraints; prices/costs; agronomic technology characteristics; innovation profitability; adopter/network thresholds; land and water rights; parcel location/distance; freshwater availability; irrigation production functions and return flows; policy/credit/subsidy assumptions
MAS_Platform_Technology: Custom MAS–cellular automata model; recursive/mixed-integer programming; C++ object-oriented implementation; spatial grid with hydrological submodel
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3 model philosophy; Sec. 4.1–4.11 model implementation/software; Figs. 1–2
Coordination_Mechanism: Innovation diffusion through social/spatial networks; endogenous land/water rental or purchase markets; auction/market clearing; shared irrigation-return-flow feedback.
Communication_Mechanism: Decentralised exchange/observation of innovation information between farm households; market/bid-based land and water transactions; environment-mediated hydrological feedback.
Information_Shared: Innovation/adoption information; land/water offers and prices; neighbourhood experience; water availability and return-flow effects
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Land; irrigation water rights and freshwater allocation; technology adoption; farm investment/production decisions
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Allocate scarce land and water among heterogeneous farms through decentralised markets while representing technology diffusion and maintaining household feasibility/income.
Conflict_Resolution: Endogenous land/water markets and auctions reallocate resources; market prices and agent profitability determine transactions rather than a central allocator.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Neighbouring farm households compete for offered land and water rights; innovators and laggards differ in access/profitability and adoption timing.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Freshwater rights and availability; upstream/downstream section; return flows; crop-water production functions; land/water market conditions; profitability and availability of water-saving technologies
Agricultural_Outcomes: Simulates innovation diffusion, farm income, farm exits/structural change, farm-size evolution and adoption of modern crop/irrigation technologies under Mercosur/policy scenarios.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Models reallocation of land and water rights and adoption of water-saving irrigation; special high-purchase scenarios speed diffusion and increase income, while informal rental arrangements can hinder investment in perennial/water-saving technologies.
Environmental_Outcomes: Represents irrigation-water use and hydrological return-flow feedback; supports analysis of improved land-use practices and natural-resource degradation.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Endogenous adoption of water-saving irrigation and improved land-use practices, plus decentralised land/water market reallocation.
Quantitative_Results: The model represents 5,400 farm households over ~667 km². Under ideal technical change, about half of total irrigated area shifts to water-saving techniques within 10 years, versus about one-fifth under bandwagon diffusion. Under bandwagon communication, almost 6% of commercial-farm laggards exit per year. Robustness checks showed <1% variation in average income/labour across repeated runs except innovator-group income (~6%).
Tradeoffs_Reported: Faster innovation/resource reallocation can raise income and water-saving adoption but also accelerates structural change and unequal outcomes between early adopters and laggards; decentralised markets may improve efficiency while changing farm viability.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 7 Selected simulation results; Figs. 3–7; Sec. 8 Conclusions and outlook
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Calibration/robustness analysis; Comparative policy/scenario evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: Spatial MAS–CA representation of an empirical Chilean agricultural region under Mercosur, innovation, credit/subsidy and land/water-market scenarios.
Data_Source: Farm surveys/records; experimental-station agronomic results; expert opinion; field observations; regional/spatial farm data; hydrological/public-works study data; literature-derived technology parameters
Experimental_Scenarios: Mercosur versus non-Mercosur; ideal, bandwagon and no-technical-change diffusion; credit/subsidy policies; alternative land/water market arrangements; repeated robustness runs.
Baselines_Comparators: Observed 1996 land/water market values used for calibration; comparison among ideal, bandwagon and pessimistic/no-technical-change scenarios.
Evaluation_Metrics: Technology adoption/saturation; irrigated area under water-saving methods; aggregate and household-group income; farm exits; farm-size distribution; land/water prices and quantities; robustness across repeated runs
Evaluation_Results: The model reproduces 1996 land/water prices and quantities reasonably; diffusion and farm-income trajectories are strongly affected by behavioural heterogeneity/social communication. Water-saving irrigation adoption is much slower under bandwagon diffusion than idealised diffusion, and structural change is substantially larger among laggard commercial farms.
Evaluation_Scale: ~667 km²; 5,400 farm households (90% campesino); 2.5-ha grid cells; 20 hydrological sections; 32 candidate innovations; 20-year scenario horizon.
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Environmental modelling; Other — behavioural assumptions; Other — market-data limitations
Reported_Limitations: Key behavioural responses such as farm exit under rising land opportunity costs rely partly on ad hoc assumptions because empirical household-response data were unavailable; land/water market emergence remains incompletely understood; predictive capacity is strongly constrained by assumptions about human decision-making.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Verify results with improved empirical data; improve understanding of efficient land/water-market emergence; further test this model class and integrate richer ecological and economic processes.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 4.6–4.11; Sec. 5 Calibration and robustness; Sec. 7; Sec. 8 Conclusions/outlook
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B12). Pre-2010 foundational study retained under IC7. Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: SINUSE: A multi-agent model to negotiate water demand management on a free access water table
Authors: S. Feuillette; François Bousquet; Patrick Le Goulven
Geographical_Context: Kairouan groundwater table, central Tunisia; study zone downstream of the El Haouareb dam
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Groundwater management; Common/free-access resource governance; Farm investment and land use
Study_Objective: Build the SINUSE multi-agent model to represent local resource–user and farmer–farmer interactions driving groundwater overexploitation, test demand-management interventions, and support negotiation of integrated groundwater management.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Explain and explore groundwater overexploitation as an emergent result of farmer investment, imitation, land/well interaction and shared aquifer dynamics, and assess management interventions.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Coordination/negotiation support framework; Policy-evaluation framework
Agent_Types: Farmer agents; plot/spatial entities; private/collective irrigation perimeter entities; well/borehole entities; groundwater-table zones
Agent_Roles: Farmers invest in irrigation, choose crops, imitate neighbours, exchange plots and messages, sometimes cooperate to build wells, and react to economic/resource conditions; wells/plots and groundwater entities mediate extraction and water-table feedback.
Decision_Mechanism: Field-observation-derived behavioural rules for crop/investment/well decisions; neighbourhood imitation; plot exchange/cooperative well construction; annual financial/resource assessment; groundwater balance feedback
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Farmer agents make local investment, cropping, land-exchange and well decisions using bounded behavioural rules and neighbourhood information; no central controller allocates groundwater.
Input_Information: Farm cash and labour; land area/location; crop and market parameters; neighbouring functioning/abandoned wells; groundwater depth/accessibility; well/borehole status; irrigation efficiency; seasonal water demand; social/field-observed behavioural rules
MAS_Platform_Technology: SINUSE implemented in Cormas (Common-pool Resources and Multi-Agent Systems) simulation environment
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 2 Case study; Sec. 3.1 modelling approach; Sec. 3.2 general model; Sec. 3.3 entities
Interaction_Type: Communication; Information sharing; Cooperation; Competition; Coordination
Coordination_Mechanism: Neighbour imitation; direct farmer messaging; temporary land exchange; cooperative well construction; shared groundwater feedback; exploratory management interventions.
Communication_Mechanism: Direct/message communication between neighbouring farmers plus environment-mediated interaction through wells, plots and the common groundwater table.
Information_Shared: Neighbour well success/failure and locations; requests/offers for plot exchange; proposals for joint well construction; local resource conditions
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Groundwater extraction; well investment; irrigated land/plot access; irrigation technology and crop water demand
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Explore how decentralised users can reduce groundwater overexploitation and assess/communicate the effects of demand-management interventions rather than centrally allocate the aquifer.
Conflict_Resolution: Cooperation/plot exchange can resolve individual access constraints; management scenarios change technology or behavioural rules; the model is intended as a negotiation support tool for stakeholders.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Private irrigators independently expand wells/irrigated area on a free-access aquifer, producing aggregate overexploitation and long-term inter-user/intergenerational competition.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Groundwater depth/accessibility; well/borehole availability; farm land/cash/labour; crop choice and seasonal water demand; irrigation efficiency; neighbour well information; investment thresholds
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 2 Case study; Sec. 3.2–3.4; Fig. 3 and interaction procedures; Sec. 4 management scenarios
Agricultural_Outcomes: Simulates farm investment, irrigated-area expansion, crop activity, land exchange and long-term farmer economic trajectories under changing groundwater conditions and management tools.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: More efficient drip irrigation improves farmer results but does not necessarily reduce groundwater pressure because efficiency gains can induce additional investment/irrigated-area expansion.
Environmental_Outcomes: Groundwater-table decline and overexploitation are the principal environmental outcomes; local social and resource interactions materially change aggregate aquifer dynamics.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Demand-management scenarios including efficient drip irrigation and behavioural/management-rule changes; stakeholder negotiation supported by the transparent MAS.
Quantitative_Results: Sensitivity experiments confirm that removing local interactions such as imitation changes global dynamics. In one drip-irrigation scenario, improved irrigation efficiency worsens resource sustainability because improved farm returns stimulate further investment; in a second behavioural scenario, aquifer outcomes differ little from reference while farmer results improve. The paper reports that >75% of farmers sell all plots within 10 years under an unrealistic land-market mechanism, versus <5% reporting any plot sale in field surveys, exposing a model limitation.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Improving irrigation efficiency can increase farm profitability yet worsen groundwater sustainability through rebound/expansion effects; demand management must balance farmer welfare with long-term aquifer conservation.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3.4 Results; Sec. 4 Use of the model; Fig. 7–8; Sec. 5 Discussion/conclusion
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Sensitivity analysis; Model credibility/validation assessment; Scenario analysis
Evaluation_Environment: Cormas-based SINUSE simulation of irrigator–aquifer dynamics in the Kairouan groundwater system.
Data_Source: Field surveys/interviews of representative farmers; hydrogeological studies; observed farming/well practices; crop/economic information; rainfall/climate series; field-derived behavioural hypotheses
Experimental_Scenarios: Reference dynamics; removal of local interactions such as imitation; parameter sensitivity; alternative efficient-drip-irrigation behavioural scenarios; other management interventions.
Baselines_Comparators: Reference simulation and field-observed qualitative/quantitative patterns; management scenarios compared against reference.
Evaluation_Metrics: Groundwater level/depth; functioning/new wells; irrigated/farm activity; farmer economic outcomes/debt; land exchanges; sensitivity of dynamics; qualitative realism/robustness
Evaluation_Results: The model reproduces major qualitative system dynamics and demonstrates that local non-economic interactions matter, but some socio-economic mechanisms generate unrealistic debt/land-market outcomes; management scenarios reveal counter-intuitive rebound effects from irrigation efficiency.
Evaluation_Scale: Kairouan aquifer >3,000 km² (modelled sub-zone); multi-year farmer/well/plot simulation with repeated stochastic experiments and sensitivity analysis.
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Environmental modelling; Other — unrealistic socio-economic/land-market rules; Other — transferability
Reported_Limitations: Many socio-economic procedures rely on assumptions; simulated land exchange/debt can be unrealistic; important hydrogeological parameters remain uncertain; the model is highly case-specific and must be used with its limits clearly understood.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Return to the field to validate behavioural assumptions with farmers/stakeholders; improve farmer income-use/land-exchange behaviour and hydrogeological parameters; socially validate implemented behaviours; test transfer to other groundwater systems.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3.4 Results; Sec. 3.5 credibility; Sec. 4; Sec. 5 Discussion/conclusion
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B14). Pre-2010 foundational study retained under IC7. Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: Agent based simulation of a small catchment water management in northern Thailand: Description of the CATCHSCAPE model
Authors: Nicolas Becu; Pascal Perez; Andrew Walker; Olivier Barreteau; Christophe Le Page
Geographical_Context: Small agricultural catchment in northern Thailand with upstream/downstream irrigation schemes and villages
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Crop and farm management; Catchment governance; Agricultural livelihoods
Study_Objective: Develop the CATCHSCAPE multi-agent model to integrate catchment biophysical dynamics with farmer and irrigation-manager decisions so upstream–downstream water conflict, negotiation and scenario impacts can be explored transparently.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Explore catchment-scale irrigation allocation and livelihood consequences emerging from farmer decisions, canal management and negotiation between irrigation managers under alternative conflict/climate scenarios.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Coordination/negotiation mechanism; Decision-support/exploratory framework
Agent_Types: Farmer agents; canal-manager agents; plot/crop entities; canals/weirs/river entities; village/irrigation-scheme entities
Agent_Roles: Farmers choose crops and manage cash/labour/water expectations; canal managers control weirs, ration water and negotiate transfers with other managers; reactive biophysical entities simulate hydrology, crops and water delivery.
Decision_Mechanism: Farmer linear-programming crop choice with cash/labour/water constraints; experience-based water expectation; manager rationing and rule-based inter-canal negotiation; biophysical crop/water dynamics
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Farmers make local crop/resource decisions; canal managers have autonomous operational and negotiation rules at multiple management levels; physical water flows constrain all decisions.
Input_Information: Farm cash/labour; crop profitability; farmer water expectations/experience; crop water demand and yield; rainfall/climate; canal/river flows; plot position; canal shortages; manager satisfaction/shortage ratios
MAS_Platform_Technology: CATCHSCAPE implemented with the Cormas multi-agent simulation framework; spatial 44×45 grid and integrated biophysical submodels
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 2 integrative/MAS approach; Sec. 3.1 spatial representation; Sec. 3.2 cognitive/reactive agents; Sec. 3.3–3.6 dynamics/decisions
Interaction_Type: Communication; Information sharing; Cooperation; Competition; Negotiation; Coordination
Coordination_Mechanism: Hierarchical canal management and rationing; manager-to-manager water-transfer negotiation; upstream/downstream requests; farmer water-expectation feedback; shared catchment hydrology.
Communication_Mechanism: Direct/message-like requests and negotiation between canal managers, plus environment-mediated interaction through shared canal/river flows.
Information_Shared: Canal water shortages/satisfaction; requests for additional water; upstream/downstream availability; farmer water expectations and irrigation conditions
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water; canal/weir operation; crop/farm resource allocation; catchment water distribution
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Allocate scarce canal water across upstream/downstream users and sustain farm livelihoods while exploring how negotiated management changes system outcomes.
Conflict_Resolution: Canal managers ration locally and negotiate water transfers across canals/irrigation schemes; downstream requests can trigger upstream sharing depending on shortage criteria.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Upstream and downstream canals/farmers compete for limited dry-season water; farmer cash/labour/water constraints also compete across crop choices.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Canal/river water availability; crop water requirements; farmer expected water supply from past experience; plot/canal position; climate/rainfall; manager shortage/satisfaction criteria
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3.4 decision-making; Sec. 3.5 irrigation management; Sec. 3.6 modelling sequences; manager negotiation description
Agricultural_Outcomes: Simulates crop choice/yield, dry-season cultivation, farm cash/livelihood categories and distributional effects of irrigation-management scenarios.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Negotiated canal management changes distribution of scarce irrigation water and can reduce inequitable upstream dominance; theft/conflict scenarios expose losses in effective water management and livelihood outcomes.
Environmental_Outcomes: Represents catchment water depletion/availability and interactions between agricultural withdrawals and hydrological conditions.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Negotiated multi-level irrigation management, rationing and scenario testing of alternative governance/climate conditions.
Quantitative_Results: The model contains 327 farmer agents on a 44×45 spatial grid. Baseline and alternative scenarios are simulated for 10 years with 20 stochastic repetitions. Simulated crop spatial patterns overlap remote-sensing observations with about 80% accuracy, and average simulated yields agree with reference data with at least 70% accuracy. In the baseline, upstream canals can irrigate roughly 65% of plots in the dry season versus about 20% downstream.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Catchment management balances upstream versus downstream irrigation access and aggregate production versus distributional equity; stronger control/negotiation can improve sharing but depends on simplified behavioural assumptions.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 4.1–4.4 simulation results; Table 1; Sec. 5 Discussion/conclusion
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Scenario comparison; Model authentication/validation assessment

Title: Suitability of Multi-Agent Simulations to study irrigated system viability: application to case studies in the Senegal River Valley
Authors: Olivier Barreteau; François Bousquet; Claude Millier; Jacques Weber
Geographical_Context: Senegal River Valley irrigated systems, West Africa
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Irrigated-system viability; Collective organisation; Credit and farm coordination
Study_Objective: Assess whether the SHADOC multi-agent virtual irrigated system can be used as a simulation laboratory to study how individual behaviour, collective rules and environment jointly influence irrigated-system viability.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Explore how coordination patterns among farmers/groups, water/credit institutions and environmental conditions generate viable or non-viable irrigated-system trajectories.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Coordination/organisation framework; Theory-building/virtual-laboratory method
Agent_Types: Farmer agents; autonomous group agents for water allocation, credit and pumping management; plots; watercourses/canal; pumping-station entities
Agent_Roles: Farmers cultivate plots, seek water/credit, exchange information/services and cooperate through friendship networks; group agents autonomously manage water allocation, credit and pumping and communicate with farmers/groups; infrastructure entities deliver water.
Decision_Mechanism: Rule-based individual behaviour and collective institutional rules; friendship-network cooperation; group-level credit/water/pumping procedures; scenario-defined rule combinations and stochastic events
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Farmer and group agents are autonomous, maintain their own system representations and goals, perceive environmental state/messages, and act/communicate at individual and collective organisational levels.
Input_Information: Plot/water state; water availability; farmer goals and inputs/labour priorities; friendship/cooperation networks; credit/debt relations; group membership/rules; pumping/canal state; scenario environment and rule parameters
MAS_Platform_Technology: SHADOC multi-agent virtual irrigated-system model developed through companion modelling; rule-based object/agent simulation
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3.1 Choice of MAS model; Sec. 3.2 From field to model; Figs. 2–3
Interaction_Type: Communication; Information sharing; Cooperation; Competition; Coordination
Coordination_Mechanism: Autonomous group-level water allocation, credit and pumping management; farmer friendship/service networks; multi-level collective rules; environment-mediated water delivery.
Communication_Mechanism: Direct messages between farmer and group agents plus information/service exchange through friendship networks; agents also perceive shared environmental state.
Information_Shared: Water availability and allocation; credit/debt state; cooperation/service requests; group relations; farmer opinions/representations
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water; credit; pumping management; plot cultivation; collective irrigated-system organisation
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maintain irrigated-system viability/longevity by coordinating water and credit access under combinations of individual behaviour, collective rules and environmental conditions.
Conflict_Resolution: Collective group rules and friendship/cooperation networks mediate water/credit access; scenario experiments test whether particular rule configurations avoid early system collapse.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Farmers and groups compete/cooperate over limited water, credit and pumping capacity; heterogeneous goals can generate coordination conflict.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Water availability and canal/plot position; collective water-allocation rules; farmer goals/input priorities; pumping state; group membership/relations; external income and scenario parameters
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 3.1–3.2; agent/group representation; Sec. 4.2 viability classification; Sec. 4.3 theory-building
Agricultural_Outcomes: Measures continued plot cultivation and irrigated-system longevity under alternative combinations of farmer goals, collective rules and environment; heterogeneous coordination affects system persistence.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Focuses on viability of collective water/credit organisation rather than a single efficiency metric; viable scenarios sustain cultivated plots and resource access for more cropping seasons.
Environmental_Outcomes: Represents irrigation-water availability/delivery as a constraint on long-term system viability; no broader environmental impact metric is quantified.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Collective rules and coordination structures for water allocation/pumping/credit intended to maintain viable use of the irrigated system.
Quantitative_Results: Scenarios are repeatedly simulated and classified by longevity/viability. For 72 scenarios allowing outside income, heterogeneous goal populations yielded 13 non-viable versus 10 slightly-viable/viable cases; moderately heterogeneous populations 7 versus 16; homogeneous populations 17 versus 9. Repeated sets of 20 simulations produced stable viability classifications despite high within-scenario stochastic variation.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Some heterogeneity supports risk sharing and viability, but strong heterogeneity can create water-access coordination conflicts; homogeneous populations simplify scheduling yet can also be less viable.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Sec. 4.2 viability classification; Sec. 4.3 theory-building; Table 3; Sec. 5 Conclusion
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Repeated stochastic experiment; Scenario classification/theory-building
Evaluation_Environment: SHADOC virtual irrigated-system laboratory representing Senegal River Valley organisation and infrastructure.
Data_Source: Field studies/interviews and observed institutional/irrigation-system organisation in the Senegal River Valley; rule/scenario sets derived from companion-modelling work
Experimental_Scenarios: Random sample of scenarios defined as environment + individual rules + collective rules; repeated simulations across varying farmer-goal heterogeneity and external-income conditions.
Baselines_Comparators: Cross-scenario comparison of different individual/collective rule configurations; no single conventional algorithmic baseline.
Evaluation_Metrics: Number/proportion of cultivated plots over cropping seasons; simulation longevity; proportion of long-enduring/viable simulations; stability of viability classification across repeated simulation sets; communication/water-use indicators
Evaluation_Results: High between-scenario variation supports discrimination of viable rule configurations, while high within-scenario randomness requires repeated simulation. Viability classification is repeatable; moderate rather than extreme goal heterogeneity is associated with more viable outcomes in the reported example.
Evaluation_Scale: Virtual Senegalese irrigated system with farmer, group and infrastructure agents; random scenario sample; each scenario simulated 100 times in five sets of 20 repetitions.
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation; Uncertainty; Reproducibility/data availability; Other — heuristic/theory-building purpose
Reported_Limitations: The model is intended as a heuristic virtual laboratory rather than a predictive tool; stochastic trajectories mean one simulation cannot determine viability; simulation-derived theories are not validated by simulation alone and require confrontation with new field evidence.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Carry out external/field validation and legitimacy assessment; use simulation-generated hypotheses to guide new thematic field research; further investigate rule configurations and controls that keep systems on viable trajectories.
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B16). Pre-2010 foundational study retained under IC7. Closely related to the SHADOC/Senegal River Valley research line; exact Study_Family_ID deferred to Step 5.
